claims.text: The high-entropy effect alone does not guarantee intrinsic thermal stability in nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal alloy nanoparticles.
Nanoparticle stability is critically dependent on suppressing chemical short-range order and avoiding percolation-driven phase separation.
High surface-to-volume ratio can trigger phase separation in nanoparticles through effects absent in bulk systems.
Annealing between 600 K and 1000 K is above the predicted order-disorder transition temperature for relevant atomic pairs.
A temperature gradient under the stated conditions allows surface diffusion to dominate.
Negative mixing interactions produce SRO clusters and networks involving preferred atomic pairs such as Cr-Hf.
SRO clusters act as nucleation sites for phase separation or intermetallic precipitation.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr exhibits no phase change and less than a 7% decrease in thermal conductivity up to 1300 K.
High nanoparticle surface energy lowers the activation barrier for SRO formation.
Strong Cr-Hf attraction leads to ordering and precipitate formation at temperatures as low as 620 K.
SRO in nanoparticles can rapidly evolve into percolating clusters with a fractal dimension of approximately 2.4.
SRO and percolating ordered clusters alter the vibrational density of states and increase thermal conductivity.
SRO-driven percolation can cause premature decomposition or phase transformation in nanoparticles.
The nanoparticles will show a rapid increase in thermal conductivity because ordered clusters percolate.
The initial conductivity increase will be followed by a sharp decrease.
B2 or sigma phases will form in nanoparticles at temperatures significantly below the bulk order-disorder transition temperature.
Theoretical models assuming random atomic distributions fail to account adequately for SRO effects on thermal conductivity.
Particle sizes above 100 nm suppress surface-driven SRO kinetics sufficiently for the bulk stability model to hold.
Positive enthalpy of mixing for all elemental pairs prevents SRO and makes the bulk stability model applicable.
External pressure can stabilize the fcc phase of CoCrFeMnNi at high temperature.

contradictions.description: The intervention characterizes 600–1000 K as above a relevant order-disorder transition and as inducing SRO, whereas the cited Cr-Hf calculation predicts an ODTT near 1120 K and reports that the low-temperature precipitate vanishes by 620 K. Thus the stated temperature relation and direction of ordering are not internally reconciled.
